---
title: "AI competency map: classical AI topics in EP"
---

::: {.callout-warning}
Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision. The examples below describe research,
much of it in simulation; none of it is a recommendation for patient care.
:::

Many AI courses organize the field into the same competency areas: machine learning, Bayesian networks and other
graphical models, logic, search, planning and game playing, Markov decision processes, reinforcement learning, and AI
and society. This page shows how each area connects to cardiac electrophysiology (EP) and mapping, where this course
already teaches it, and where it does not yet. Use it to plan a reading path, or to see which parts of an AI
curriculum an EP engineer will use first.

## Machine learning

**The idea.** Fit a model to examples so that it predicts labels or values for new inputs, and measure how well it
does on data it has not seen.

**Why it matters in EP.** Electrograms, ECGs, maps and images are large, labeled or labelable data sets. The course
uses supervised learning to annotate electrograms and detect drivers ([m35](modules/m35-machine-learning.qmd)),
classify rhythms from the surface ECG ([m37](modules/m37-ai-ecg.qmd)), triage wearable alerts
([m38](modules/m38-wearables-monitoring.qmd)), learn on mapping meshes ([m39](modules/m39-ai-electrograms-maps.qmd)),
segment images ([m40](modules/m40-ai-imaging-substrate.qmd)), locate arrhythmia origins
([m41](modules/m41-ai-origin-localization.qmd)), add physics to learning
([m42](modules/m42-physics-informed-ml.qmd)) and pretrain foundation models
([m43](modules/m43-foundation-models-llms.qmd)).

**What an EP engineer needs first.** Patient-wise splits, external validation and calibration
([m35](modules/m35-machine-learning.qmd)). A retrospective accuracy is not evidence of clinical benefit
([m45](modules/m45-ai-evidence-regulation.qmd)).

## Bayesian networks

**The idea.** A directed graph whose nodes are variables and whose arrows say what depends on what, with a
probability table at each node. Inference runs Bayes' rule along the graph.

**Why it matters in EP.** The simplest Bayesian network has two nodes, a condition and a test result. Its inference
is the positive predictive value of [m35](modules/m35-machine-learning.qmd#eq-m35-ppv), and in odds form the
likelihood ratios of [m48](modules/m48-imaging-workflow.qmd). A chain such as "AF present, the device alerts, a triage
filter keeps the alert" is how [m38](modules/m38-wearables-monitoring.qmd) treats the alerts' PPV as the prior for
the triage step. The Gaussian process in [m41](modules/m41-ai-origin-localization.qmd) is Bayesian inference
over a whole function: it gives an estimate and an uncertainty at every candidate pacing site.

**A lesson the graph makes visible.** Multiplying the likelihood ratios of two tests assumes they are independent
given the condition. Two tests that share a failure cause, such as the same motion artifact, are not, and
multiplying their evidence overstates certainty. A Bayesian network draws that shared cause as a node.

**Not yet in the course.** Learning network structure from data, and inference in networks larger than a chain.

## Graphical models

**The idea.** The family that contains Bayesian networks (directed graphs), Markov random fields (undirected
graphs) and hidden Markov models (chains of hidden states that emit observations). The graph says which variables
are conditionally independent, which makes inference and learning tractable.

**Why it matters in EP.** Signals that pass through a fixed sequence of states suit hidden Markov models. One early
method delineated the P wave by modeling each beat with a hidden Markov model, then used P-wave features to separate
82 patients with documented AF from 63 controls, with sensitivity and specificity between 65% and 70%
[@clavier2002]. Neighboring sites on a map are not independent either; the graph networks of
[m39](modules/m39-ai-electrograms-maps.qmd) use the same mesh structure but are trained as deterministic networks,
not as probabilistic graphical models. Knowing the difference helps when a method claims calibrated uncertainty.

**Not yet in the course.** Hidden Markov models, Markov random fields and their inference algorithms.

## Logic

**The idea.** Knowledge written as explicit rules, from if-then statements to formal logic, so that a conclusion can
be traced to the rules that produced it and every rule can be tested.

**Why it matters in EP.** Much of EP reasoning is already written as rules. A classic stepwise algorithm for a
regular wide-QRS tachycardia applies four criteria in order; in its prospective analysis of 554 tachycardias the
four steps together had sensitivity 0.987 and specificity 0.965 for ventricular tachycardia [@brugada1991]. Device
and wearable alerts often fire only after a rule such as "k positive windows in a row", which changes sensitivity
and PPV as much as the model does ([m38](modules/m38-wearables-monitoring.qmd)). AI agents run under a policy that
says which actions run, which need a person's approval and which are refused, and guardrails written as rules sit
outside the model ([m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd)) [@rebedea2023guardrails].

**Why engineers like rules.** A rule can be read, reviewed and tested exhaustively; a learned model cannot. Systems
in EP often combine both: a learned score and a rule-based gate around it.

## Search

**The idea.** Explore a space of states or options in an order that guarantees, or approximates, the best answer:
breadth-first, shortest-path, best-first and heuristic search.

**Why it matters in EP.** Activation spreading through tissue is a shortest-time problem: fast marching computes
arrival times in a single ordered sweep, as Dijkstra's algorithm does for shortest paths on a graph
([m30](modules/m30-capstone-mini-mapping-system.qmd)) [@sethian1996]. Distances on a mapping mesh are found by shortest paths
along its edges ([m41](modules/m41-ai-origin-localization.qmd)). Retrieval searches a corpus for the passages a
language model should cite ([m43](modules/m43-foundation-models-llms.qmd)), and an agent searches over tool calls
([m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd)). Searching many model designs against one validation set is also search, and it
leaks the validation set into the result ([m35](modules/m35-machine-learning.qmd),
[m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd)).

## Markov decision processes

**The idea.** A Markov decision process (MDP) has states, actions, transition probabilities and rewards; a policy
maps each state to an action, and the best policy maximizes expected total reward over a sequence of decisions.

**Why it matters in EP.** Mapping is sequential: each new point, pacing site or image changes what is worth doing
next. Active pace-mapping in [m41](modules/m41-ai-origin-localization.qmd) chooses the next pacing site from a
Gaussian process; one Bayesian-optimization method reached 3.9 ± 3.6 mm with 8.0 ± 4.0 sites in simulation
[@meisenzahl2024]. That is a one-step-ahead (greedy) answer to a sequential decision problem; an MDP formulation
would also weigh how today's choice changes the value of later ones, and would need a model of transitions and a
reward that someone has to choose.

**Not yet in the course.** The MDP formalism, value functions and the Bellman equations.

## Reinforcement learning fundamentals

**The idea.** Reinforcement learning (RL) learns a policy for an MDP from reward, by trial and error, without being
told the right action. Q-learning, for example, learns the value of each action in each state.

**Why it matters in EP, and why only in simulation.** Trial and error is not acceptable on patients, so RL in EP
research runs in simulated tissue. In one study, a Q-learning agent moved over two-dimensional left atrial models
built from LGE MRI of AF patients and placed lesions to terminate simulated AF; it terminated AF in 84% of training
cases and 72% of test cases, all in simulation [@muizniece2021]. Such results show what a simulator rewards, not what
helps patients: the policy is only as good as the simulator ([m33](modules/m33-capstone-digital-twin.qmd),
[m42](modules/m42-physics-informed-ml.qmd)) and the reward its designers chose. This course does not teach RL for
therapy choices.

**Not yet in the course.** Q-learning, policy gradients and their pitfalls (reward misspecification, simulator gaps).

## Planning and game playing

**The idea.** Planning finds a sequence of actions that reaches a goal; game playing searches against an opponent,
choosing moves that are best against the opponent's best reply (min-max).

**Why it matters in EP.** AI agents plan, act and observe in a loop, one tool call at a time, under a step limit and
with human approval for any write ([m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd)) [@yao2023react]. Game playing's min-max idea
returns in adversarial robustness: training a model to resist small malicious input changes can be written as a
min-max problem in which an attacker maximizes the loss and the defender minimizes it [@madry2018]. The fast
gradient sign method of [m46](modules/m46-trustworthy-ai.qmd) is the simplest such attacker
[@goodfellow2015fgsm].

## AI and society

**The idea.** Who benefits and who is harmed, what evidence is enough, how data are protected, who is accountable,
and how people stay in control.

**Why it matters in EP.** The course treats this as engineering: study designs and reporting
([m45](modules/m45-ai-evidence-regulation.qmd)), device regulation ([m36](modules/m36-prototype-to-product.qmd)),
fairness, uncertainty and robustness ([m46](modules/m46-trustworthy-ai.qmd)), de-identification and data governance
([m47](modules/m47-data-deployment-engineering.qmd)), and human approval for every write action of an agent
([m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd)). For example, an AI-ECG model trained on a cohort that was 96.2% non-Hispanic
white kept AUCs between 0.931 and 0.961 across racial and ethnic subgroups of its test cohort, and its authors
recommended reporting performance by race, ethnicity, age and sex [@noseworthy2020].

## Reading paths

- **Probabilistic reasoning:** [m35](modules/m35-machine-learning.qmd) (Bayes' rule) →
  [m48](modules/m48-imaging-workflow.qmd) (likelihood ratios) → [m38](modules/m38-wearables-monitoring.qmd) (chained
  alerts) → [m41](modules/m41-ai-origin-localization.qmd) (Gaussian processes) →
  [m46](modules/m46-trustworthy-ai.qmd) (uncertainty).
- **Search and sequential decisions:** [m30](modules/m30-capstone-mini-mapping-system.qmd) (fast marching) →
  [m41](modules/m41-ai-origin-localization.qmd) (shortest paths, active pace-mapping) →
  [m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd) (agent loops and plans).
- **Rules, robustness and society:** [m38](modules/m38-wearables-monitoring.qmd) (alert rules) →
  [m44](modules/m44-agentic-ai.qmd) (policies and guardrails) → [m46](modules/m46-trustworthy-ai.qmd) (adversarial
  min-max, fairness) → [m45](modules/m45-ai-evidence-regulation.qmd) and
  [m47](modules/m47-data-deployment-engineering.qmd).

## What the course does not cover yet

Graphical models beyond Bayes' rule and simple chains, the MDP formalism, and reinforcement learning are named on
this page but not taught in a module. Adding modules for them would change the curriculum and needs the author's
approval.
